lesson.title: Filling In the Hole for Good: Continuous Extension
lesson.summary: A continuous extension takes a function with a removable discontinuity and builds a new, slightly larger function that agrees with the original everywhere and is continuous at the formerly missing point too.
lesson.body:
When a function f has a removable discontinuity at c, the limit lim(x to c) f(x) exists as some finite value L, even though f itself is undefined at c or takes the wrong value there. A continuous extension of f is a new function F, defined by F(x) = f(x) for every x not equal to c, and F(c) = L. Because L is exactly the value the continuity test at c requires, F automatically satisfies all three parts of the definition of continuity at c: F(c) is defined, lim(x to c) F(x) exists, and it equals F(c). The extension does not change f anywhere it was already defined and working; it only supplies the one missing or corrected value.

The name extension is deliberate: F extends the domain of f to include the point c, while agreeing with f everywhere the original function was already defined. In practice, once the algebra has been simplified, the continuous extension often turns out to have a much cleaner formula than the original, since the expression that produced the removable discontinuity, typically a shared factor causing a 0/0 form, cancels away and leaves a simpler function that happens to already be defined at c.

Worked example: let f(x) = (x^2 - 9)/(x - 3), defined for every real x except x = 3. As shown earlier, factoring gives f(x) = x + 3 for x not equal to 3, and lim(x to 3) f(x) = 6. The continuous extension of f is F(x) = x + 3, now taken to be defined for every real number, including x = 3, where F(3) = 6 matches the limit exactly. Away from x = 3, F(x) = f(x) by construction, so nothing about the original function's behavior has changed, and F is continuous everywhere, including at the formerly troublesome point.

A well known second example is the sinc-type function f(x) = sin(x)/x, defined for every real x except x = 0. Substituting x = 0 gives the indeterminate form 0/0, so f(0) is undefined, but it is a standard, well established result that lim(x to 0) sin(x)/x = 1. The continuous extension is F(x) = sin(x)/x for x not equal to 0, and F(0) = 1. This extended function shows up throughout mathematics and signal processing precisely because it is continuous everywhere, with no gap left at the origin, unlike the original formula on its own.

Continuous extension only works when the underlying discontinuity is removable, which is why this concept depends so directly on that one. If the one-sided limits at c disagree, as in a jump discontinuity, there is no single value L that could serve both sides, and no continuous extension exists. If a one-sided limit is infinite, or if the function oscillates without settling, there is likewise no finite value to assign. A continuous extension is possible exactly when, and only when, a genuine, finite limiting value was there all along, simply waiting to be assigned to the missing point.

It is common in practice to blur the line between f and its continuous extension F, calling both of them simply f once the extension is understood, since the extended function is really just the honest, complete version of the same rule. Formally keeping them distinct, however, matters when comparing domains, since f and F technically differ at exactly the one point c where f was undefined or wrong, even though every calculation involving limits, derivatives, or integrals near c gives identical answers for either one.
